intro: Build the document in Chrome, Safari, or Edge, then either submit it to your organization's template gallery or keep a master copy. Personal accounts reuse a master copy by choosing File > Make a copy for every new document.
tldr: Google Docs has no separate template feature for Mac. You work in Chrome, Safari, or Edge at docs.google.com.
Work or school account: Template gallery > your organization > Submit template, then pick the file and submit it.
Personal account: keep a master document, then use File > Make a copy for every new document.
Google's help does not describe submitting a custom template from a personal Gmail account.
The File menu shortcut is ⌃⌥F (Ctrl+Option+F). Use it to reach Make a copy from the keyboard.

blocks.text: Before you start: Google Docs on Mac runs in a browser

Google Docs has no separate template feature for macOS. You open docs.google.com in a browser, and every template step happens on that page. Chrome, Safari, and Edge all work for normal editing, so use the one you already trust.

That matters for two things. The menus you need, like File, sit inside the Docs page, not in the macOS menu bar at the top of the screen. And Google's Mac shortcut list uses ⌘ for most keys, but the File menu shortcut uses Control and Option, written ⌃⌥F, so read the symbols carefully.
Which template path fits your account

Your account type decides which path you take. Google's help defines work or school accounts as accounts that do not end in @gmail.com. Those accounts can submit a template to their organization's gallery. Personal Gmail accounts reuse a master document instead, because Google's help does not describe custom template submission for them.

blocks.caption: Which path to use, based on the account you sign in with.

blocks.text: Check the path before you build. It decides whether you need a clean copy in a gallery or a master file in your Drive.
Create a template in a work or school account

Start with a finished document, not a rough draft. Put placeholders in square brackets, like [Client name] and [Date], so the people who use the template know what to replace. Keep the layout simple. Heavy custom formatting is harder to fix later.

Submission depends on sharing. You need permission to change the file's sharing settings. If the file's sharing stops viewers and commenters from downloading it, the submission fails. Shared drives add their own limits, so a template on a shared drive can be blocked even when the file looks fine.

Use the copy option when you want a clean template in the gallery and a working file for yourself. Tick the box to submit a copy, and your original stays yours to keep editing. It is a small choice that avoids cleanup later.
Make a reusable template in a personal account

A personal account has no gallery to submit to, so your template is a file you keep and copy. The How-To Geek guide from January 2020 suggests a simple setup. Add the word Template to the file name, put the file in a folder, and use File > Make a copy for each new document. The guide is dated, and its screenshots are from 2019, but the copy command it describes is still in Google's current help.

Naming is the part people skip. A name like Template: Weekly meeting notes sorts together in Drive and stands out from real work. Keep masters in one folder, and do not type into them. Type only into copies.
A worked example: a weekly meeting notes template

Say you run a weekly team meeting. You build one document with a date heading, three fixed sections called Wins, Blockers, and Decisions, and a table for action items with columns for Owner and Due date. You save it as Template: Weekly meeting notes in a Templates folder.

Before you rely on it, test the master. Make one copy, fill in fake names, and check that the table keeps its columns and the headings keep their styles. Then delete the test copy so nobody finds it later.
Each Monday, open the master, choose File > Make a copy, and rename the copy with the date. The copy opens as its own file. The master never changes, which is the whole point of the workflow.

In the copy dialog, change the name first and choose a location second. The Copy comments and suggestions box is optional. Leave it off for a fresh start. Tick it only when the master holds review notes that should follow each copy.
Common mistakes when you make a Google Docs template

items: Editing the master. Every new copy starts from the master, so a typo there reaches every future document. Open the master only to change the template.
Leaving sample text in. Replace every placeholder before you share, or teammates will fill in your sample words by mistake.
Skipping the sharing check. Submission fails when the file's sharing stops viewers and commenters from downloading it.
Trusting the Google gallery as yours. Templates in Google's own gallery are made by Google. Your masters live in your Drive or in your organization's gallery.
Naming copies Untitled. Names like Copy of Template make search useless. Put the date and the topic in the name.

blocks.text: Watch for the Add-on label too. If Add-on appears beside a template, you may need to install an add-on first. Install it before you open the template, or the file may not behave as the author intended.
Use Google Docs offline on a Mac

Offline editing needs Google Chrome or Microsoft Edge, with the Google Docs Offline extension turned on. Private browsing cannot be used. Google's offline help names Chrome, Edge, and ChromeOS, and it does not mention macOS. Test offline mode on your Mac before you travel with a template.

The setup starts in Google Drive. Click Settings at the top right, click Settings again, and turn on Offline. Only one account per browser profile can have offline turned on, and your administrator can disable offline sync. Very large files can fail with an error, so keep long templates lean.
Shortcuts for the template workflow

Two shortcuts matter most for templates. ⌃⌥F opens the File menu from the keyboard, so you can get to Make a copy without hunting along the top of the page. ⌘/ shows the full shortcut list, which helps when you forget a key.
Google's shortcut page lists no shortcut for Make a copy and none for a new document. Do not spend time searching for one. Use ⌃⌥F, then the menu, and keep your attention on the template.
When a template is the wrong tool

A template helps when the structure repeats, such as weekly notes, client letters, or the same report layout each quarter. It does not help for one-off documents. If you write a structure once, a blank page is faster than a master you will never copy again.

Recreating documents is a real cost, even if the numbers are rough. A 2019 M-Files Global IIM Benchmark Report survey of more than 1,500 office workers found that 83% of organizational staff are forced to recreate lost documents that already exist. M-Files is a document management company, and the survey covers office documents in general, not Google Docs.
What to do next

Once the template works, add the parts people expect. [Add a header and footer in Google Docs on Mac](/how-to/add-a-header-and-footer-in-google-docs) so every copy carries the same branding. For long reports, [add a table of contents](/how-to/add-a-table-of-contents-in-google-docs) before you make the master.

If you write for a living, the [Google Docs page for writers on Mac](/for/writers/google-docs) covers templates and offline editing in more depth. For help while you work, see the [AI assistant for Google Docs on Mac](/apps/google-docs).

faq.question: Is there a Google Docs app for Mac that makes templates?
faq.answer: No separate Google Docs app handles templates on a Mac. Google Docs runs in the browser, so you use Chrome, Safari, or Edge. Templates live in the Template gallery or in your Drive, depending on your account.

faq.question: Can I create a template in Google Docs with a personal Gmail account?
faq.answer: Yes, by keeping a master document and reusing it with File > Make a copy. Google's help does not describe submitting a custom template from a personal account, and third-party guides disagree, so do not rely on a gallery submission.

faq.question: Do I need Google Workspace to use templates?
faq.answer: No. Personal accounts can use the master copy method. Work or school accounts get the gallery submission path, as long as the file's sharing settings allow it.

faq.question: Will my team see my template?
faq.answer: Only if you share it or submit it. A master in your Drive stays private until you share it. Submitting to your organization's gallery makes it available through that gallery, so check the sharing settings first.

faq.question: Can Lazur create the template for me?
faq.answer: No. Lazur does not click buttons or operate other apps for you. Hold Option and Command and ask where something is, and Lazur points at it. Ask how to do something, and Lazur guides you one click at a time, waiting for each click.

faq.question: What is the fastest way to start a new document from a template?
faq.answer: Open the master, press ⌃⌥F to open the File menu, and choose Make a copy. Name the copy, pick a location, and click OK. After setup, that is the whole process.

task: Create a reusable template in Google Docs on Mac
appliesTo: Google Docs in Chrome, Safari, or Edge on macOS, for work and personal accounts
requirements: A Mac with Chrome, Safari, or Edge installed
A Google account, with a work or school account for the gallery submission path
Edit access to the document you want to turn into a template
Permission to change sharing settings, needed only for gallery submission

steps.name: Open Google Docs in your browser
steps.text: Open Chrome, Safari, or Edge on your Mac and go to docs.google.com. Sign in with the account that should own the template, not whichever account you used last.
steps.tip: Chrome is the safest choice if you plan to work offline, since offline mode needs Chrome or Edge.

steps.name: Build the document you want to reuse
steps.text: Write the document with its layout, headings, tables, and fixed text in place. Replace variable content with placeholders in square brackets, such as [Client name] and [Date].
steps.tip: Use one placeholder style everywhere, so nobody misses one.

steps.name: Open the Template gallery
steps.text: From the Docs home screen, click Template gallery at the top right. The gallery holds Google's own templates, so you can see what a finished template looks like.

steps.name: Open your organization's tab
steps.text: In the gallery, click your organization's name. This tab holds the templates your organization has published and the option to submit your own.

steps.name: Click Submit template
steps.text: Click Submit template. If you do not see it, your account may be a personal one. Use the personal account steps below instead.

steps.name: Select your document and open it
steps.text: Click Select a document, choose the file you built in step two, and click Open.

steps.name: Choose whether to submit a copy
steps.text: Tick the box to submit a copy if you want to keep the original as your working draft. Leave it unticked to submit the original file itself.
steps.tip: Tick the box when you want a clean template in the gallery while your working file stays yours.

steps.name: Pick a category and submit
steps.text: Choose a category that fits the template, then click Submit. If submission fails, check the file's sharing settings before you try again.

steps.name: Create the personal master
steps.text: For a personal account, make the template yourself. Finish the document, click the file name at the top, and add the word Template, such as Template: Weekly meeting notes.

steps.name: Put the master in a folder
steps.text: In Google Drive, create a folder called Templates and move the master into it. Keep that folder for masters only, so you never type into one by accident.

steps.name: Make a copy for each new document
steps.text: Open the master, then choose File > Make a copy. In the dialog, type the new name, choose where to save it, and leave Copy comments and suggestions unticked for a fresh start. Click OK.

steps.name: Check the copy and leave the master alone
steps.text: The copy opens in its own tab with the new name. Fill in the placeholders, then close the tab. Never type into the master, because every future copy starts from it.
steps.tip: Keep the master closed while you work on copies, so you do not type into it by mistake.

troubleshooting.problem: No Submit template button in the gallery
troubleshooting.fix: Google's help defines work or school accounts as accounts that do not end in @gmail.com. Check the email you signed in with. If you use a personal Gmail account, use the master copy method instead.

troubleshooting.problem: Submission fails with a sharing error
troubleshooting.fix: You need permission to change the file's sharing settings. Also check that viewers and commenters can download the file. On a shared drive, ask the drive manager whether sharing limits block access.

troubleshooting.problem: The template shows an Add-on label
troubleshooting.fix: Google's help says you may need to install an add-on first. Install it, then open the template again.

troubleshooting.problem: Old comments show up in every copy
troubleshooting.fix: Untick Copy comments and suggestions in the Make a copy dialog. The box is optional, so it stays unticked unless you want the notes carried over.

troubleshooting.problem: Offline mode does not work on my Mac
troubleshooting.fix: Use Chrome or Edge with the Google Docs Offline extension turned on. Private browsing cannot be used. Google's offline help does not mention macOS, so test it before you rely on it.

troubleshooting.problem: Make a copy is missing from the File menu
troubleshooting.fix: Open the file itself, not a preview. Press ⌃⌥F to open the File menu and look again. If the option is still missing, ask the file owner what access you have.
